What is Form 16?

Form 16 is the TDS certificate your employer must give you by 15 June for the previous financial year. Part A shows tax deducted and deposited quarter by quarter; Part B shows the salary break-up, exemptions, deductions and the tax computation. It is the main document for filing ITR-1, and it must match Form 26AS / AIS.

Is F&O trading income business income?

Yes — futures and options are treated as non-speculative business income, so you file ITR-3, can deduct expenses, and can carry forward losses for 8 years (set off against any business income). Intraday equity is speculative business (losses only against speculative gains, carried 4 years). Turnover for audit is computed from absolute profit and loss.

Yes, it is likely a bad idea to buy a property with a mortgage, live in it for 1 year, and then go traveling for 2-5 years. Here are some reasons why:

2. Property maintenance: While you are away, the property may require maintenance and repairs, which can be costly and time-consuming to manage from a distance.
3. Vacancy rates: If you are away for an extended period of time, the property may be vacant, which can lead to a decrease in rental income and increased expenses for property management.
4. Market conditions: The real estate market can be unpredictable, and it is possible that the value of your property may decrease while you are away.
5. Travel expenses: Traveling can be expensive, and you may not have the financial resources to cover the costs of your trip while also making mortgage payments and managing your property.

Does financing a portfolio on margin affect the variance of a portfolio?

Variance of a single asset is defined as follows: σ2 = Σi(Xi - μ)2 where Xi's represent all the possible final market values of your asset and μ represents the mean of all such market values.  The portfolio's variance is defined as σp2 = Σiwi2σi2 where, σp is the portfolio's variance, and wi stands for the weight of the ith asset.  Now, if you include the borrowing in your portfolio, that would classify as technically shorting at the borrowing rate. Thus, this weight would (by the virtue of being negative) increase all other weights. Moreover, the variance of this is likely to be zero (assuming fixed borrowing rates). Thus, weights of risky assets rise and the investor's portfolio's variance will go up. Also see, CML at wikipedia.

This is a key indicator of profitability for insurance companies. A lower loss ratio is better. Expense ratio - The ratio of operating expenses to premiums collected. This measures the efficiency of underwriting and administrative costs. A lower expense ratio is better. Combined ratio - The sum of the loss ratio and expense ratio. A combined ratio under 100% indicates an underwriting profit. Risk selection - Metrics to evaluate how well the AI model is able to identify and underwrite good risks while avoiding bad risks. This could include metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. Claim denial rate - The percentage of claims that are denied. A reasonable denial rate indicates the AI model is functioning properly and not paying out illegitimate claims. Customer satisfaction - Metrics based on customer feedback and Net Promoter Score to measure customer experience with the AI insurance product. Higher satisfaction is obviously better. Market share - The percentage of the target market that the AI insurance product captures. Higher market share indicates more customers and growth potential. Profit margin - The percentage of premiums collected that remain as profit after paying claims and expenses. Higher profit margins indicate a more sustainable and profitable product. So in summary, the key things an AI insurance company would look at are profitability metrics like loss ratio, expense ratio and profit margin, as well as risk selection metrics, customer satisfaction, and market share. A combination of these metrics can help evaluate how well the AI product is performing and identify areas for improvement.

A savings account linked to FDs so that balances above a threshold are automatically moved into fixed deposits (earning FD rates) and broken in units when you need cash. You get near-FD returns with savings-account liquidity; broken deposits earn interest for the period held, sometimes with a small penalty.

Is selling only shares you bought with margin on a margin/unsettled cash purchase free ride?

I'm not 100% sure, but I don't think it would be considered a free ride. The idea of a free ride is that you are engaging in a transaction when you do not actually have the money available to cover it, since the broker is technically giving you a 3 day loan whenever you purchase your stock (3 day rule to settle.) However, if you are using a margin account, and you have enough credit available, then you are not actually using unsettled assets, but rather an additional line of credit which was granted to you. You would just need to make sure that your total transactions are less than your purchasing power. That's my take on it anyway. I hope that helps, and hopefully someone can confirm or reject what I have said.

How does the process of assignment work for in-the-money Options?

When the strike price ($25 in this case) is in-the-money, even by $0.01, your shares will be sold the day after expiration if you take no action. If you want to let your shares go,. allow assignment rather than close the short position and sell the long position...it will be cheaper that way. If you want to keep your shares you must buy back the option prior to 4Pm EST on expiration Friday. First ask yourself why you want to keep the shares. Is it to write another option? Is it to hold for a longer term strategy? Assuming this is a covered call writing account, you should consider "rolling" the option. This involves buying back the near-term option and selling the later date option of a similar or higher strike. Make sure to check to see if there is an upcoming earnings report in the latter month because you may want to avoid writing a call in that situation. I never write a call when there's an upcoming ER prior to expiration. Good luck. Alan

Question:
what makes real world assets special

Real-world assets are unique in several ways: 1. Tangibility: Real-world assets, such as real estate, commodities, and physical goods, have a tangible presence in the world. They can be seen, touched, and experienced, which is not the case with digital assets. 2. Scarcity: Real-world assets are often scarce, meaning there is a finite supply. This scarcity can drive up demand and increase the value of the asset. 3. Liquidity: Real-world assets can often be easily bought and sold, which makes them more liquid than many digital assets. This liquidity can be important for investors who want to quickly convert their investment into cash. 4. Regulation: Real-world assets are often subject to regulation, which can provide a level of protection for investors and increase the trust in the asset. 5. Diversification: Investing in real-world assets can provide diversification for investors, as the value of these assets can be less correlated with other asset classes. 6. Security: Real-world assets can provide a sense of security, as they are tangible and can be physically secured. This can be important for investors who are concerned about the security of their investments. Overall, real-world assets offer a unique combination of tangibility, scarcity, liquidity, regulation, diversification, and security, which can make them an attractive investment option for many investors.

Why would you elect to apply a refund to next year's tax bill?

The refund may offset your liability for the next year, especially if you are a Schedule "C" filer.  By having your refund applied to the coming year's taxes you are building a 'protection' against a potentially high liability if you were planning to sell a building that was a commercial building and would have Capital Gains. Or you sold stock at a profit that would also put you in the Capital Gain area.  You won a large sum in a lottery, the refund could cushion a bit of the tax. In short, if you think you will have a tax liability in the current year then on the tax return you are filing for the year that just past, it may be to your benefit to apply the refund. Question:
what is the best way to analyse earnings management in the financial statements of banks ?

Earnings management in the financial statements of banks can be analyzed through various methods, including: 1. Comparative analysis: Compare the bank's financial statements over a period of time to identify any unusual changes or trends in earnings. This can help identify if the bank is managing earnings to meet certain targets or expectations. 2. Ratio analysis: Analyze financial ratios such as the return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE) to identify any unusual fluctuations or trends in earnings. This can help identify if the bank is engaging in earnings management to improve these ratios. 3. Cash flow analysis: Analyze the bank's cash flow statement to identify any unusual changes or trends in operating, investing, or financing activities. This can help identify if the bank is managing earnings by manipulating cash flows. 4. Disclosures: Review the bank's disclosures in the financial statements to identify any unusual accounting policies or practices. This can help identify if the bank is engaging in earnings management through these policies or practices. 5. External factors: Consider external factors such as market conditions, regulatory changes, and economic trends that may impact the bank's earnings. This can help identify if the bank is engaging in earnings management to mitigate the impact of these factors. Overall, a combination of these methods can be used to analyze earnings management in the financial statements of banks.

Tax on insurance payment due to car deemed as total loss?

DJClayworth's response is generally correct. You wouldn't have to pay taxes on insurance benefits, since those are in fact bringing you whole to what you've lost. However, in some cases you do need to consider taxes. Specifically, if the insurance payout is higher than your cost basis in the lost property. While you may think that this never happens (why would the insurance company pay more than what it cost you?), it in fact quite frequently does. Specific example would be a car used in your business. If you used your car as part of your business and deducted car depreciation on your tax return - your cost basis was reduced by the depreciation. Getting a full car cost payout form insurance would in fact constitute taxable income to you for the difference between your cost basis (adjusted for the depreciation) and the payout. Another example would be collectibles. Say you bought a car 20 years ago at $5000, you maintained it well during the years (assume you spend another $5000 on repairs), and it is now insured at FMV of $50000. But, alas, it got destroyed by a mountain lion who climbed over the fence and pushed it over a cliff. You got a $50000 payout from your insurance company (because you insured it for full FMV coverage, as a collectible should be insured), of which $40000 will be taxable to you. There may be more specific cases where insurance payouts are (partially) taxable. However, as a general rule, they're not, as long as they're at or below your cost basis level.

What is EBITDA?

Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation — operating profit before financing and non-cash charges, used to compare the core profitability of businesses with different debt and asset bases. How is the opening-day price of a stock decided?

When a stock is going to become public there's a level of analysis required to figure out the range of IPO price that makes sense. For a company that's somewhat mature, and has a sector to compare it to, you can come up with a range that would be pretty close. For the recent linkedin, it's tougher to price a somewhat unique company, running at a loss, in a market rich with cash looking for the next great deal. If one gives this any thought, an opening price that's so far above the IPO price represents a failure of the underwriters to price it correctly. It means the original owners just sold theirvshares for far less than the market thought they were worth on day one. The day of IPO the stock opens similar to how any stock would open at 9:30, there are bids and asks and a price at which supply (the ask) and demand (bid) balance. For this IPO, it would appear that there were enough buyers to push the price to twice the anticipated open and it's maintained that level since.  It's possible to have a different system in which a Dutch auction is used to make the shares public, in theory this can work, it's just not used commonly.

* Be patient: Remember that healing takes time. Don't rush the process and be kind to yourself.

If you are looking at long-term investments then you can look to Dheer's answer and see that it doesn't matter whether the money is large or small, the return will be the same. If I was managing your hypothetical portfolio opening a position for 1,000,000 shares, it can cause the price to go up significantly because I have to execute the order very carefully in order to not tip my hand to the market that I want a million shares. Then later when it comes time to sell, I will lose a percentage to the price drop as I start flooding the market with available shares.

Why do stocks priced above $2.00 on the ASX sometimes move in $0.005 increments?

Like in the US, more flexibility is extended to hidden orders. Australia has taken an aggressive approach to hidden orders in the direction of lower ticks. Aussies have a rich financial that evolved differently than the Dutch custom more familiarly known in the UK and US. They, like Chicago evolved out of commodities trade rather than trade.  When commodities are worth nearly nothing per unit, larger precision comes naturally. For the Dutch, it was the opposite.  A single ship would trade in 1/64 share or for the largest vessels, 1/128 share.  Here, there's no point to high precision.  New York, founded by the Dutch specialized in logistics just the same.   To a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail, so both Chicago, Australia, and other financial systems built by commodities rather than trade have extended the higher precision logic to everything else, and pricing is fantastic. It should not be a surprise why Australia has taken a lead in pushing infinite precision.

Explain donut economics

Donut economics is a concept developed by economist NAME_1 that challenges the traditional economic model of a growing, expanding economy. The traditional model is often visualized as an upward-sloping curve that represents increasing GDP, with the goal of maximizing economic growth. NAME_2's donut economics model, on the other hand, is shaped like a donut with a hole in the middle. The hole represents the social and ecological thresholds that must be avoided to ensure a sustainable and equitable economy, while the outer ring represents the essential needs and human rights that must be met to create a just and thriving society. The model suggests that economic growth should be focused on meeting the needs of people within the ring, while also avoiding the negative impacts of economic activity on the environment and social equity. This approach prioritizes the well-being of people and the planet over the pursuit of endless growth. Donut economics is intended to provide a more holistic and equitable framework for economic decision-making that takes into account the needs of all people and the health of the planet. It aims to shift the focus of economics from maximizing growth to creating a more just and sustainable economy that benefits everyone.

Effect of country default on house prices?

It could be a a way to preserve the value of your money, but depends upon various factors. If a country defaults, and it leads to hyper-inflation, by definition that means that money loses its purchasing power.  In even simpler terms, it cannot buy as much tomorrow as I could today. Assuming some kind of re-stabilization of the economy and currency, even with several more zeros on the end, it is conceivable that the house would subsequently sell for an appropriately inflation adjusted amount, as other in-demand physical goods may. If you're operating as a sole proprietor, you may be exposing yourself to liability: debts and judgments against your business can put your personal assets at risk! So, if you're intending to continue and grow your side work in the future, you ought to consider the LLC sooner than later. It's also an important legal decision and you should consider seeking a professional opinion. The Wall Street Journal has a brief guide titled How to Form an LLC.  Here are some notable excerpts: A limited liability company, or LLC,   is similar to a partnership but has   the legal protections of personal   assets that a corporation offers   without the burdensome formalities,   paperwork and fees.   [...]   Some states charge annual fees and   taxes that can diminish the economic   advantage of choosing to become an   LLC. Among LLC advantages:   pass-through taxation – meaning the   profits and losses “pass through” the   business to the individuals owning the   business who report this information   on their own personal tax returns. The   result can be paying less in taxes,   since profits are not taxed at both   the business level and the personal   level. Another plus: Owners aren’t   usually responsible for the company’s   debts and liabilities.   [...] Also check out onstartups.com's Startup 101: Should You Form An Inc. or An LLC? I like Muro questions! No, I don't think they do.  Because for me, as a personal finance investor type just trying to save for retirement, they mean nothing. This type of coverage can provide reimbursement for medical expenses, lost wages, and property damage. By opting into this coverage, you can avoid the stress and financial burden of suing the other driver personally, as your insurance company will handle the claims process. It's important to understand exactly what your insurance policy covers and does not cover, and to do an insurance checkup annually to ensure you are not over or under-insured.

What is an STP and an SWP?

A Systematic Transfer Plan moves a fixed sum periodically from one fund to another (typically liquid → equity) to average into the market after a lump-sum windfall. A Systematic Withdrawal Plan redeems a fixed amount each month — e.g. ₹30,000 a month from a ₹50 lakh corpus earning 8% leaves about ₹70 lakh after 20 years, because growth exceeds the withdrawal. Each STP/SWP leg is a taxable redemption.

Checkout the worksheet on page 20 of Pub 535.  Also the text starting in the last half of the third column of page 18 onward.  The fact that you get a W-2 is irrelevant as far as I can see.  Your self-employment business has to meet some criteria (such as being profitable) and the plan needs to be provided through your own business (although if you're sole proprietor filing on Schedule C, it looks like having it in your own name does the trick).  Check the publication for all of the rules. There is this exception that would prevent many people with full-time jobs on W-2 from taking the deduction: Other coverage. You cannot take the deduc­tion for any month you were eligible to partici­pate in any employer (including your spouse's) subsidized health plan at any time during that month, even if you did not actually participate. In addition, if you were eligible for any month or part of a month to participate in any subsidized health plan maintained by the employer of ei­ther your dependent or your child who was un­der age 27 at the end of 2014, do not use amounts paid for coverage for that month to fig­ure the deduction. (Pages 20-21).  Sounds like in your case, though, this doesn't apply. (Although your original question doesn't mention a spouse, which might be relevant to the rule if you have one and he/she works.) The publication should help.  If still in doubt, you'll probably need a CPA or other professional to assess your individual situation.

If the gift is not exempt from income to the receiver - it is no longer a gift and the receiver is paying income taxes, not the donor. The situation you describe is a classic tax evasion scheme. If someone does it consistently and regularly (as a receiver, donor, or both) - he would likely end up in jail.

Explain how the law of supply and demand affects the economy

The law of supply and demand states that prices of goods and services are driven by the interaction between the availability of a product and the amount of demand for it. When prices increase, it signals to producers to create more of the product, as there is a higher demand, and when prices decrease, it signals to consumers to buy more of the product as it has become more affordable. This process helps to balance the supply and demand of goods and services, keeping prices relatively stable and helping ensure an efficient allocation of resources.

How can IV give an indication of the markets opinion about a stock when there's no such thing as IV for a stock?

Since near-term at-the-money (ATM) options are generally the most liquid, the listed implied vol for a stock is usually pretty close to the nearest ATM volatility, but there's not a set convention that I'm aware of.  Also note that for most stocks, vol skew (the difference in vol between away-from-the-money and at-the-money options) is relatively small,  correct me if I'm wrong, IV is the markets assessment that the stock is about 70% likely (1 Standard Deviation) to move (in either direction) by that percent over the next year. Not exactly.  It's an annualized standard deviation of the anticipated movements over the time period of the option that it's implied from.  Implied vol for near-term options can be higher or lower than longer-term options, depending on if the market believes that there will be more uncertainty in the short-term.  Also, it's the bounds of the expected movement in that time period. so if a stock is at $100 with an implied vol of 30% for 1-year term options, then the market thinks that the stock will be somewhere between $70 and $130 after 1 year.  If you look at the implied vol for a 6-month term option, half of that vol is the range of expected movement in 6 months.
